questions.stem: Which specialized structure allows electrical signals to spread directly from one cardiac muscle cell to the next?
questions.explanation: Gap junctions form low-resistance channels that pass ions and current between adjacent myocytes, allowing cell-to-cell impulse spread. Desmosomes anchor cells mechanically but do not conduct electricity.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Intercalated discs contain gap junctions plus which mechanical anchoring structure?
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs house both gap junctions (electrical coupling) and desmosomes (mechanical coupling that holds cells together during contraction). This combination supports synchronized beating.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: The statement "the heart behaves as a functional syncytium" means that:
options: Each myocyte contracts independently of its neighbors
There is no electrical coupling between cardiac cells
The atria function as one coordinated unit and the ventricles as another
Only the pacemaker cells generate contractile tension
questions.explanation: Because of extensive gap junctions, the atrial muscle depolarizes and contracts as a single unit, and the ventricular muscle does the same. The fibrous skeleton prevents direct electrical spread from atria to ventricles.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Which structural feature is found in cardiac muscle but NOT in skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs with gap junctions and desmosomes are unique to cardiac muscle. Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle, but it is involuntary and typically has a single central nucleus.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle cells characteristically contain:
options: Nuclei clustered at each cell end
questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are short, branching cells with a single (occasionally two) centrally placed nucleus. Peripheral multiple nuclei are a feature of skeletal muscle fibers.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Functionally, gap junctions provide:
options: Low-resistance pathways for ion flow between cells
A direct blood supply to each myocyte
questions.explanation: Gap junctions are connexon channels that allow ions and small molecules to pass, creating a low-resistance electrical pathway. Desmosomes, not gap junctions, provide the mechanical attachment.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Depolarization spreads rapidly across the myocardium because of:
options: Gap junctions combined with conduction along the sarcolemma
questions.explanation: The impulse travels along each cell's sarcolemma and jumps to the next cell through gap junctions, producing rapid whole-tissue depolarization. There are no synapses within the working myocardium.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Autorhythmic cells are defined as cells that:
options: Generate impulses spontaneously without external stimulation
Fire only when stimulated by the autonomic nervous system
Are found only in the ventricular walls
Maintain a perfectly stable resting membrane potential
questions.explanation: Autorhythmic (pacemaker) cells depolarize themselves spontaneously and repeatedly, setting the heart's intrinsic rhythm. The ANS only modifies this intrinsic activity.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: What is the role of the autonomic nervous system in the heartbeat?
options: It has no influence on cardiac electrical activity
It directly depolarizes ventricular muscle cells
It modifies the rate and force of the intrinsic rhythm
questions.explanation: The heartbeat is generated intrinsically by the conduction system; sympathetic and parasympathetic input only speeds up, slows down, or strengthens the inherent rhythm. The heart continues beating without neural input.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: The myocardium is composed of which tissue type?
questions.explanation: The myocardium is the thick muscular middle layer of the heart made exclusively of cardiac muscle, the only tissue type found in the heart itself.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of cardiac muscle?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is involuntary, striated, and composed of branching cells; it cannot be consciously controlled. Voluntary control is a property of skeletal muscle.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Cardiac myocytes are packed with mitochondria primarily because:
options: Their continuous contractile activity demands large amounts of ATP
Mitochondria store the calcium for contraction
questions.explanation: The heart works continuously and relies almost entirely on aerobic metabolism, so dense mitochondrial packing supplies the ATP for contraction and ion pumping. Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not mitochondria.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Sarcomeres, the contractile units of cardiac muscle, are located:
questions.explanation: Sarcomeres run from Z-line to Z-line within each cardiac cell and contain the actin–myosin contractile machinery. Intercalated discs and gap junctions are coupling structures, not contractile units.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: The desmosomes of the intercalated disc serve to:
options: Mechanically hold adjacent cells together during contraction
Delay conduction between atrium and ventricle
questions.explanation: Desmosomes are anchoring junctions that resist the mechanical stress of repeated contraction. Ion conduction is the job of gap junctions in the same disc.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Direct electrical spread from atrial muscle into ventricular muscle is prevented by the:
options: Gap junctions at the AV ring
questions.explanation: The non-conducting fibrous skeleton (annulus fibrosus) electrically isolates atria from ventricles, so the impulse must pass through the AV node and His bundle. This isolation is what makes one-way, organized conduction possible.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: If gap junction function were significantly reduced in ventricular myocardium, the most likely result would be:
questions.explanation: Gap junctions are the low-resistance route for current flow; reducing them increases electrical resistance and slows propagation. Slowed conduction predisposes to dyssynchrony and re-entry arrhythmias.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Cardiac cells are electrically coupled by gap junctions and mechanically coupled by:
questions.explanation: The intercalated disc contains both junction types: gap junctions for electrical continuity and desmosomes for mechanical strength. Synapses and motor end plates belong to the nervous system, not cardiac muscle.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Within a cardiac cell, the electrical signal reaches the cell interior rapidly via the:
questions.explanation: T-tubules are sarcolemmal invaginations that carry the depolarization deep into the cell so the entire myofibril is activated nearly simultaneously. Gap junctions connect cells; T-tubules penetrate each cell.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: The atria depolarizing and contracting "as one unit" is attributable to:
options: A common nerve supplying every atrial cell simultaneously
Gap junctional coupling between atrial myocytes
The AV valves holding the cells together
The pericardium compressing the walls equally
questions.explanation: Electrical coupling through gap junctions makes the atrial muscle behave electrically as a syncytium, so a single SA nodal impulse activates all atrial cells in sequence within milliseconds.
tags: Cardiac Muscle Structure & the Electrical Syncytium

questions.stem: Compared with working (contractile) myocardial cells, SA nodal cells:
options: Have abundant myofibrils and a stable resting potential
Have no electrical connection to the atrial muscle
Have sparse contractile elements and depolarize spontaneously
questions.explanation: SA nodal cells are small and specialized, lack strong contractile filaments, and generate impulses automatically. Their job is pacing, not force generation. ---

questions.stem: In excitation–contraction coupling, which ion entering through the T-tubules triggers the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release its stored calcium?
questions.explanation: Calcium entering during the action potential plateau triggers additional calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (calcium-induced calcium release), producing a large cytosolic calcium rise that activates contraction.

questions.stem: Released calcium initiates contraction by binding directly to:
questions.explanation: Calcium binds troponin, the calcium-sensing regulatory protein on the actin filament. This troponin–calcium complex then moves tropomyosin off the binding sites.

questions.stem: When calcium binds its regulatory site, tropomyosin responds by:
options: Blocking the actin filaments more tightly
Shifting position to expose myosin-binding sites on actin
questions.explanation: The troponin–calcium complex pulls tropomyosin away from the actin binding grooves, allowing actin–myosin cross-bridge formation. ATP is hydrolyzed by myosin, not tropomyosin.

questions.stem: Cardiac relaxation occurs when:
options: Calcium is removed from the cytosol and resequestered (mainly into the SR)
questions.explanation: Contraction ends as calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum and extruded from the cell; tropomyosin then re-covers the actin binding sites. Rising cytosolic calcium causes contraction, not relaxation.

questions.stem: The primary function of T-tubules in cardiac muscle is to:
options: Carry the electrical signal rapidly into the interior of the cell
Anchor the heart to the pericardium
questions.explanation: T-tubules are sarcolemmal invaginations that transmit the surface action potential to the cell core, synchronizing SR calcium release throughout the myocyte. Calcium storage belongs to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.stem: Actin–myosin cross-bridge cycling in cardiac muscle requires:
questions.explanation: Calcium uncovers the binding sites and ATP powers the myosin cross-bridge stroke. Without both, contraction cannot occur regardless of electrical excitation.

questions.stem: Which event must occur first for the ventricles to contract?
questions.explanation: Electrical activity precedes mechanical activity: the ventricles must be depolarized before they can contract. Valve closure is a consequence of pressure changes that follow contraction.

questions.stem: The sarcoplasmic reticulum of cardiac muscle functions to:
options: Conduct the action potential between cells
Anchor the Z-lines of adjacent sarcomeres
questions.explanation: The SR is the intracellular calcium store; it releases calcium on stimulation and resequesters it for relaxation. Cell-to-cell conduction is a gap junction function.

questions.stem: The term "excitation–contraction coupling" describes the linkage between:
options: Electrical depolarization of the membrane and mechanical contraction
The ECG and the pulse wave
Systole and diastole of the atria only
questions.explanation: It is the sequence by which the action potential (electrical event) leads to calcium release and cross-bridge cycling (mechanical event). Depolarization initiates muscle action, and contraction follows a short, predictable delay.

questions.stem: The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump maintains ion gradients by:
options: Moving sodium and potassium against their concentration gradients using ATP
Allowing both ions to diffuse passively down their gradients
Pumping potassium out and sodium in equally
questions.explanation: The pump actively extrudes Na⁺ and brings K⁺ in, preserving the gradients that make resting potential and repeated action potentials possible. Without it, gradients would dissipate and the cell could not keep firing.

questions.stem: The rapid upstroke (phase 0) of the ventricular action potential is produced mainly by:
options: Sodium influx through fast Na⁺ channels
questions.explanation: Fast sodium channels open at threshold and Na⁺ rushes in, rapidly driving the membrane toward positive values. K⁺ efflux repolarizes; Ca²⁺ influx sustains the plateau.

questions.stem: The plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential results from:
options: Slow calcium influx roughly balancing potassium efflux
questions.explanation: During the plateau, slow Ca²⁺ channels admit calcium while K⁺ channels let potassium leave; the opposing currents hold the membrane near 0 mV. This plateau extends contraction and the refractory period.

questions.stem: Repolarization (phase 3) of the ventricular action potential is caused primarily by:
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open fully, so potassium leaves the cell and the potential returns toward the resting level. Na⁺ influx would depolarize, not repolarize.

questions.stem: The resting membrane potential of a ventricular muscle cell is approximately:
questions.explanation: Working ventricular cells rest near −90 mV, held stable by K⁺ permeability and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. Values near −40 to −60 mV are typical of nodal tissue, and +30 mV is the peak of the AP.

questions.stem: In a fast-response cardiac cell, the action potential fires once the membrane potential reaches threshold, approximately:
questions.explanation: Fast Na⁺ channels activate at roughly −60 to −70 mV; reaching this threshold triggers the all-or-none upstroke. 0 mV is mid-plateau and +30 mV is the peak.

questions.stem: Once fast sodium channels inactivate during the action potential, the cell:
options: Cannot be re-excited until the channels recover (refractory period)
questions.explanation: Inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes, making the cell refractory to new stimulation. This guarantees a full relaxation and refill between beats.

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized because:
options: Its action potential is too short
Its prolonged refractory period lasts almost as long as contraction
questions.explanation: The long plateau action potential keeps Na⁺ channels inactivated for most of the twitch, so a second stimulus cannot summate contractions. Skeletal muscle, with its brief AP, can undergo summation and tetanus.

questions.stem: The peak (overshoot) of the ventricular action potential reaches approximately:
questions.explanation: Sodium influx drives the membrane from −90 mV to roughly +20 to +30 mV at the AP peak. The other choices describe resting or threshold values.

questions.stem: The stoichiometry of the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase is:
options: 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in
2 Na⁺ out for every 3 K⁺ in
Na⁺ in and K⁺ out in equal amounts
1 Ca²⁺ out for every 3 Na⁺ in
questions.explanation: The pump exports 3 sodium ions and imports 2 potassium ions per ATP consumed, generating a net outward current that helps maintain the negative resting potential. The sodium–calcium exchanger (option D) is a separate transporter.

questions.stem: Drugs such as digoxin increase contractility by:
options: Increasing the amount of calcium available to the contractile machinery
questions.explanation: By inhibiting the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, digoxin indirectly raises intracellular calcium, and more calcium delivered to troponin means a stronger contraction. This illustrates how ion movement directly links electrical activity to mechanical performance. ---
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of the normal cardiac impulse pathway?
options: AV node → SA node → bundle of His → atria
SA node → Purkinje fibers → AV node → bundle branches
SA node → internodal pathways → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
Bundle of His → SA node → AV node → Purkinje fibers
questions.explanation: The impulse originates in the SA node, spreads through internodal/atrial pathways to the AV node, is delayed, then passes through the bundle of His, the right and left bundle branches, and finally the Purkinje fibers to the ventricles.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: Which structure is the normal pacemaker of the heart?
questions.explanation: The SA node generates impulses automatically at the highest intrinsic rate, so it dominates and sets the heart rhythm. All other sites can pace but only if the SA node fails.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: The SA node is located in the:
options: Left atrium near the pulmonary vein orifices
Right atrium near the junction with the superior vena cava
questions.explanation: The SA node sits in the right atrial wall near the SVC entry. Nodal tissue near the pulmonary veins is ectopic, not normal, and the septum contains the AV node and His bundle.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: The physiologic purpose of the delay in the AV node is to:
options: Allow time for ventricular filling before ventricular contraction
questions.explanation: The AV nodal delay lets the atria finish ejecting blood (atrial kick) before the ventricles depolarize and contract, optimizing preload. Without this pause, ventricular filling would be compromised.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: The AV node is located:
options: In the right ventricular free wall
In the interatrial septum near the coronary sinus ostium
questions.explanation: The AV node lies in the low interatrial septum, in Koch's triangle near the coronary sinus opening, positioned to receive the atrial impulse and pass it to the bundle of His.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: The bundle of His conducts the impulse from the AV node:
options: Through the fibrous skeleton into the interventricular septum
questions.explanation: The His bundle is the only normal electrical bridge across the electrically insulating fibrous skeleton, carrying the impulse into the ventricular septum where it divides into bundle branches.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: The right and left bundle branches course:
options: Down the interventricular septum toward the apex
questions.explanation: After the His bundle splits, the bundle branches descend along the interventricular septum and eventually subdivide into Purkinje fibers that reach the ventricular walls.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: Among the specialized conduction tissues, Purkinje fibers are distinguished by having the:
options: Fastest conduction velocity in the heart
Lowest intrinsic rate of all nodal tissue only in the atria
questions.explanation: Purkinje fibers conduct at roughly 2–4 m/s, several times faster than AV nodal tissue, which allows near-simultaneous activation of the entire ventricular mass and efficient ejection.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: After the Purkinje fibers distribute the impulse, the next cells to be activated are the:
questions.explanation: Purkinje fibers deliver the impulse to ordinary ventricular muscle cells, causing ventricular depolarization and contraction. The sequence never returns upward to atrial or nodal tissue in normal conduction.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: On the ECG, atrial depolarization is represented by the:
questions.explanation: The P wave records the spread of depolarization across both atria initiated by the SA node. The QRS and T waves reflect ventricular events.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: On the ECG, ventricular depolarization is represented by the:
questions.explanation: The QRS complex records the rapid spread of depolarization through the ventricles via the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers. The T wave records ventricular repolarization, not depolarization.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: The T wave on the ECG represents:
questions.explanation: The T wave marks recovery (repolarization) of the ventricles. Atrial repolarization occurs during the QRS and is normally hidden by that larger complex.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: The PR interval primarily reflects:
options: Conduction time from atrial depolarization through the AV node to ventricular depolarization
questions.explanation: The PR interval spans the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS and is dominated by the AV nodal delay. It measures conduction timing, not contractile duration.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: Which cardiac tissue conducts impulses most slowly?
questions.explanation: The AV node conducts very slowly (a deliberate physiologic "brake"), creating the delay that permits ventricular filling. Purkinje fibers are the fastest-conducting tissue in the heart.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: If the SA node fails to fire, the next fastest intrinsic pacemaker — the AV junction — takes over at a rate of approximately:
questions.explanation: The AV nodal/junctional tissue has an intrinsic discharge of about 40–60 bpm, making it the normal backup pacemaker. Ventricular (His–Purkinje) escape is even slower at 20–40 bpm.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: An ECG records cardiac electrical activity by:
options: Measuring voltage differences between skin electrodes and displaying them over time
questions.explanation: Surface electrodes detect the summed voltage changes of cardiac depolarization and repolarization, plotted as a waveform against time. Pressures, valve motion, and flow are measured by other modalities.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: The statement "the ECG shows timing, not contraction" means the ECG:
options: Displays only the electrical sequence and timing of activation
questions.explanation: The ECG records electrical events and their timing; it does not directly show contraction. Echocardiography is the modality that visualizes the mechanical response.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: Which imaging modality directly visualizes the mechanical contraction that follows the electrical signal?
questions.explanation: Echo images the moving myocardium, allowing direct observation of the mechanical response to electrical activation. The ECG and Holter record electrical timing only.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: The relationship between electrical activity and mechanical contraction is:
options: Electrical activity occurs first, with mechanical contraction following a short, predictable delay
They occur simultaneously with no delay
questions.explanation: Depolarization initiates the muscle action, and contraction follows after a brief electromechanical delay. This consistent sequence is why ECG timing reliably predicts mechanical events.
tags: The Cardiac Conduction System & Impulse Pathway

questions.stem: Which mechanical event immediately follows the P wave?
options: AV valve closure during ventricular systole
questions.explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarization, and atrial contraction follows it during the PR interval. Ventricular contraction waits until after the QRS. ---

questions.stem: What is the intrinsic firing rate of the SA node?
questions.explanation: The SA node generates impulses automatically at 60–100 bpm, the fastest intrinsic rate in the heart, which is why it normally serves as the dominant pacemaker.

questions.stem: What is the intrinsic rate of AV nodal (junctional) tissue?
questions.explanation: Junctional tissue discharges at about 40–60 bpm and serves as the backup pacemaker if the SA node fails. Junctional escape rhythms therefore run at 40–60 bpm with absent or retrograde P waves.

questions.stem: What is the intrinsic discharge rate of the His–Purkinje system (ventricular escape pacemaker)?
questions.explanation: The His–Purkinje network fires intrinsically at only 20–40 bpm, the slowest of the potential pacemakers, which is why ventricular escape rhythms are slow with wide QRS complexes.

questions.stem: The AV node does not normally pace the heart because:
options: It is electrically isolated from the atria
The autonomic nervous system actively blocks it
It is overdrive-suppressed by the faster-firing SA node
questions.explanation: The SA node's higher intrinsic rate depolarizes the AV node before the AV node can reach its own threshold. Suppressing a lower pacemaker with a faster one is called overdrive suppression.

questions.stem: Pacemaker (autorhythmic) cells differ from working myocardial cells in that they have:
options: A stable resting membrane potential of −90 mV
No stable resting potential — the membrane slowly depolarizes on its own until threshold
Only a prolonged refractory period and no other special features
questions.explanation: Autorhythmic cells drift spontaneously from a maximum negative value toward threshold, fire, repolarize, and repeat the cycle continuously. This pacemaker (pre)potential is the basis of the heart's intrinsic rhythm.

questions.stem: The slow spontaneous depolarization (prepotential) of SA nodal cells is generated mainly by:
options: Slow sodium influx (funny current) combined with declining potassium efflux and late calcium influx
questions.explanation: Nodal diastolic depolarization results from gradual inward Na⁺ "funny" current, decreasing K⁺ permeability, and T-type Ca²⁺ influx carrying the cell to threshold. Fast Na⁺ channels play little role in nodal firing.

questions.stem: The threshold for firing an action potential in SA nodal cells is approximately:
questions.explanation: Nodal cells reach threshold near −40 mV, at which point L-type calcium channels open and an AP is fired. −90 mV is the ventricular resting potential; +30 mV is the ventricular AP peak.

questions.stem: Although SA nodal cells lack strong contractile filaments, they fulfill their role because they are:
options: Insulating the atria from each other
The strongest-contracting cells in the atrium
Directly conducting impulses into the ventricles
Electrically connected to atrial muscle and therefore initiate atrial depolarization
questions.explanation: The SA node's automatic impulses spread through gap junctions into the surrounding atrial myocardium, making it the trigger for every normal heartbeat. Its contractile weakness is irrelevant to its pacing function.

questions.stem: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation of the SA node:
options: Has no effect on nodal firing
Slows the heart rate by decreasing the slope of the pacemaker potential
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine reduces the rate of spontaneous depolarization, so threshold is reached more slowly and firing frequency falls. It also slows AV conduction rather than speeding it.

questions.stem: Sympathetic stimulation of the SA node:
options: Increases the heart rate by steepening the slope of the pacemaker potential
Only shortens the ventricular refractory period
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine accelerates the prepotential, so threshold is reached sooner and rate rises; it also speeds AV conduction. Increased contractility (inotropy) accompanies the chronotropic effect.

questions.stem: Which electrical event immediately precedes atrial contraction (atrial systole)?
questions.explanation: Electrical activity precedes mechanical activity: atrial depolarization (P wave) triggers atrial contraction shortly afterward. The QRS relates to ventricular depolarization and contraction.

questions.stem: The SA node is the heart's dominant pacemaker because, compared with all other potential pacemaker sites, it:
questions.explanation: The rhythm belongs to whichever site fires first; because the SA node reaches threshold fastest (highest intrinsic rate), it controls the heart. Overdrive suppression keeps slower sites dormant.

questions.stem: An ECG shows a regular narrow-QRS rhythm at 55 bpm with no visible P waves. This most likely represents:
questions.explanation: Junctional rhythms run at the AV nodal intrinsic rate (40–60 bpm), are narrow-QRS, and lack sinus P waves. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular, and ventricular rhythms are wide-QRS.

questions.stem: A 46-bpm regular narrow-complex rhythm without P waves is best classified as:
questions.explanation: A rate within 40–60 bpm with absent P waves fits the AV junction's intrinsic range. Sinus bradycardia would show P waves; ventricular escape would be wide-complex and 20–40 bpm.

questions.stem: A wide-QRS rhythm at 28 bpm in a patient with complete AV block indicates the escape pacemaker lies in the:
questions.explanation: Slow (20–40 bpm) wide-QRS escape rhythms originate from His–Purkinje or ventricular tissue below the block. Junctional escapes are narrow and faster.

questions.stem: The autorhythmic cycle repeats continuously because:
options: After each action potential the membrane again drifts toward threshold and fires, repeating endlessly
Ion gradients run down and restart each cycle
Nerve input resets the membrane each beat
Calcium accumulates until the cell bursts into firing
questions.explanation: Following each AP, repolarization restores conditions for the pacemaker potential, and the slow depolarization begins again. This self-repeating loop is the intrinsic cardiac rhythm and continues without neural input.

questions.stem: If a rapid atrial tachycardia suddenly terminates, there is typically a pause before the sinus rhythm resumes. This pause reflects:
options: Complete failure of the SA node
Overdrive suppression of the lower pacemakers, which need time to recover their automaticity
questions.explanation: The fast rhythm had suppressed the sinus node and other pacemakers; once it stops, the suppressed pacemaker takes time to depolarize to threshold again. Recovery of automaticity after termination is a classic manifestation of overdrive suppression.

questions.stem: Purkinje fibers characteristically have the ______ conduction velocity but the ______ intrinsic firing rate in the heart.
questions.explanation: Purkinje tissue conducts fastest (~2–4 m/s) yet fires intrinsically slowest (20–40 bpm). Rapid conduction and slow automaticity are separate properties, and both serve synchronized ventricular activation.

questions.stem: At rest, the actual heart rate (~70 bpm) is lower than the SA node's intrinsic rate (~100 bpm) because:
options: Sympathetic dominance raises it above the intrinsic rate
The intrinsic rate is fixed at 70 bpm under all conditions
The ANS has no effect on SA nodal rate
Resting parasympathetic (vagal) tone suppresses the intrinsic rate
questions.explanation: Continuous vagal slowing holds the resting rate below the SA node's intrinsic 60–100 (nominally ~100) firing capacity. Loss of vagal tone (e.g., atropine) unmasks the faster intrinsic rate.

questions.stem: A drug that increases the SA node firing rate is said to have a positive ______ effect.
questions.explanation: Chronotropy refers to heart rate (frequency of firing); inotropy is contractile force, dromotropy is conduction velocity, and lusitropy is relaxation. Positive chronotropy = faster SA nodal discharge. ---
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Purkinje fibers are located:
options: In a subendocardial network within the ventricular walls
On the epicardial surface of the atria
questions.explanation: Purkinje fibers form a broad subendocardial network in both ventricles, receiving impulses from the bundle branches and delivering them to the working ventricular myocardium.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: The main contribution of the Purkinje system to cardiac function is:
options: Delaying the impulse for ventricular filling
Distributing the impulse rapidly to ensure synchronized ventricular contraction and efficient blood ejection
questions.explanation: By activating the ventricular mass almost simultaneously, Purkinje fibers make the ventricles contract as one unit, maximizing ejection. Delay and rhythm-setting belong to the AV node and SA node, respectively.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Compared with Purkinje fibers, conduction through the AV node is:
options: About 2–4 m/s, the same as Purkinje tissue
About 1 m/s, slightly slower than Purkinje tissue
Very slow (roughly 0.02–0.1 m/s), the slowest in the conduction system
questions.explanation: AV nodal cells are small with few gap junctions, producing markedly slow conduction — the source of the AV delay. Purkinje conduction is dozens of times faster.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Which structure transmits the impulse from the AV node into the interventricular septum?
questions.explanation: The bundle (common) of His is the continuation of the AV node that crosses the fibrous skeleton into the septum, where it divides into the right and left bundle branches.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: The left bundle branch characteristically divides into:
questions.explanation: The left bundle branch splits into anterior and posterior fascicles (plus a septal division in many hearts), whereas the right bundle descends as a single trunk. Fascicular block refers to disease of these divisions.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: In the normal heart, the only electrical connection between atrial myocardium and ventricular myocardium is the:
options: Direct left atrial–left ventricular muscle continuity
AV junction (AV node and bundle of His)
questions.explanation: The fibrous skeleton insulates the two muscle masses, so the impulse must funnel through the AV node and His bundle. Accessory pathways (e.g., in WPW) are abnormal exceptions.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: A PR interval of 0.28 seconds on the ECG indicates:
options: A normal finding in all adults
questions.explanation: A PR longer than 0.20 s signifies delayed conduction, usually at the AV node. It does not reflect SA nodal function, and 0.28 s exceeds the normal 0.12–0.20 s range.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Which region of the conduction system has the longest refractory period, an important safeguard against excessively rapid ventricular rates?
questions.explanation: The AV node's long refractory period limits how many atrial impulses reach the ventricles, protecting them from arrhythmias such as atrial flutter or fibrillation (e.g., 2:1 or higher block).
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Regarding action potential duration among conduction tissues:
options: Purkinje fibers have the shortest AP
Purkinje and ventricular APs have identical durations
Purkinje fibers generate no true AP
Purkinje fibers have the longest AP duration
questions.explanation: Purkinje action potentials are the longest, which extends their refractory period and helps prevent retrograde re-excitation of the distal conduction system.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Which potential pacemaker site has the slowest intrinsic discharge rate?
questions.explanation: The intrinsic-rate hierarchy runs from fastest to slowest: SA node (60–100) → AV junction (40–60) → His–Purkinje (20–40). The slowest site paces only when all faster sites fail.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Bachmann's bundle is best described as:
options: The fibrous partition between atria and ventricles
The continuation of the AV node into the septum
An interatrial conduction pathway that carries the impulse from the right atrium to the left atrium
The distal network within the ventricular apex
questions.explanation: Bachmann's bundle is a major internodal/interatrial tract that spreads the SA nodal impulse to the left atrium, allowing both atria to depolarize as one unit.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Vagal stimulation of the AV node will:
options: Prolong the PR interval by slowing AV conduction
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine slows AV nodal conduction and prolongs the PR interval; strong vagal tone can even produce AV block. It also slows the sinus rate rather than increasing it.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Sympathetic stimulation of the AV node produces a:
options: Shorter PR interval from enhanced AV conduction
Longer PR interval from nodal inhibition
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine speeds AV nodal conduction, shortening the PR interval while also raising rate and contractility. Sympathetic effects are uniformly "positive" (chronotropic, inotropic, dromotropic).
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: An asymptomatic endurance athlete has a resting heart rate of 48 bpm with normal sinus rhythm. The most likely explanation is:
options: Physiologic increase in vagal tone from training
questions.explanation: Aerobic training raises resting vagal tone, slowing the SA node while stroke volume increases. The rhythm remains sinus, and this is a normal adaptive finding.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: The AV node's delay is longest for impulses arriving:
options: Rapidly during the atrial fast pathway only
Prematurely, because some tissue is still refractory
questions.explanation: Premature impulses encounter partially recovered nodal tissue and conduct even more slowly (or are blocked), further lengthening the effective delay. This decremental property protects the ventricles.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Purkinje fibers "support efficient blood ejection" primarily because they:
options: Activate the entire ventricular myocardium nearly simultaneously, producing a coordinated powerful contraction
Delay the impulse to enhance preload
questions.explanation: Near-simultaneous activation makes the ventricles squeeze as a coordinated unit, maximizing stroke volume. Purkinje cells themselves contribute little force; their role is distribution of the signal.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Unidirectional (one-way) conduction from atria to ventricles is ensured by:
options: The AV valves physically pushing the impulse forward
The electrically insulating fibrous skeleton combined with the AV node acting as the sole conduit
questions.explanation: Because the fibrous skeleton blocks all other routes, the impulse can only enter the ventricles through the AV junction, which normally conducts antegrade. This architecture prevents chaotic spread.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: A wide QRS complex (>0.12 s) on the ECG suggests:
options: Slow cell-to-cell ventricular activation, as with bundle branch block or a ventricular origin
questions.explanation: When activation bypasses the rapid Purkinje system — or a bundle branch is blocked — depolarization spreads slowly muscle-to-muscle, widening the QRS. Narrow QRS implies normal fast conduction.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: In complete AV block with a wide-QRS escape rhythm at 30 bpm, the escape pacemaker is located:
options: Below the AV node, in the His–Purkinje/ventricular tissue
questions.explanation: Wide QRS at 20–40 bpm indicates a sub-His (ventricular) escape. A junctional escape would be narrow-complex and 40–60 bpm; the SA node cannot drive the ventricles in complete block.
tags: AV Node, Bundle of His & the Purkinje Network

questions.stem: Which conduction tissue has an action potential most similar to that of working ventricular muscle (a fast-response AP with a plateau)?
options: None — all conduction tissue uses calcium-driven APs
questions.explanation: Purkinje fibers generate fast-response, sodium-dependent action potentials with a plateau, closely resembling ventricular muscle APs (but longer in duration). Nodal tissue relies on slow calcium channels. ---

questions.stem: Cardiac action potentials are generated by:
options: Ion accumulation outside the cell membrane
Movement of ions through membrane channels down their electrochemical gradients
questions.explanation: An action potential is an electrical signal created by controlled ion movement (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, K⁺) through selective membrane channels. The direction and magnitude of each current determine the shape of the AP.

questions.stem: The term "membrane potential" refers to the:
options: Charge difference between the inside and outside of the cell membrane
questions.explanation: Membrane potential is the voltage created by the separation of charge across the lipid membrane. Ion gradients (mainly Na⁺ outside, K⁺ inside) maintain this difference.

questions.stem: Which ion channels participate in generating the cardiac action potential?
questions.explanation: The cardiac AP is produced by coordinated Na⁺ (fast upstroke), Ca²⁺ (plateau), and K⁺ (repolarization) channel activity. Chloride and magnesium play only minor or structural roles.

questions.stem: In the resting ventricular myocyte, membrane permeability is highest for which ion?
questions.explanation: Resting permeability is dominated by potassium channels, so the resting potential sits close to the potassium equilibrium potential (≈ −90 mV). Sodium permeability at rest is very low.

questions.stem: Which feature of the cardiac action potential is absent from the nerve action potential?
questions.explanation: Nerve APs are brief spikes with no plateau; the cardiac AP's sustained plateau (phase 2) is its distinguishing feature, built from slow Ca²⁺ influx balanced against K⁺ efflux.

questions.stem: The duration of a typical ventricular action potential is approximately:
options: The same as a nerve AP
questions.explanation: Ventricular APs last 200–300 ms, roughly 100 times longer than the 1–2 ms nerve AP. The extended duration is what supports the long contraction and refractory period of the heart.

questions.stem: The nerve action potential relies primarily on which ions?
questions.explanation: This is the classic distractor trap: the *cardiac* AP uses Na⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺, while the *nerve* AP uses mainly Na⁺ and K⁺. Calcium channel activity is what creates the cardiac plateau.

questions.stem: Inactivation of fast sodium channels during the cardiac AP results in:
questions.explanation: Once fast Na⁺ channels inactivate, they cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes, making the cell unexcitable (absolutely refractory). This prevents premature or summed contractions.

questions.stem: Potassium efflux through delayed rectifier channels produces:
questions.explanation: Outward K⁺ current carries positive charge out of the cell, restoring the negative resting potential during phases 1 and 3. Inward Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ currents produce depolarization and plateau instead.

questions.stem: The refractory period is defined as the interval during which:
options: A normal action potential cannot be elicited
Calcium accumulates in the cytosol only
questions.explanation: During the refractory period, Na⁺ (or Ca²⁺) channels are unavailable, so the cell cannot fire another full AP regardless of stimulus strength. Partial recovery later permits only weak responses (relative refractory).

questions.stem: The resting ionic gradients are characterized by:
options: Sodium high inside, potassium high outside
Sodium high outside, potassium high inside
questions.explanation: Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase maintains high extracellular Na⁺ and high intracellular K⁺. These opposing gradients power both depolarization (Na⁺ in) and repolarization (K⁺ out).

questions.stem: The direct energy source for the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump is:
questions.explanation: The pump hydrolyzes ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in against their gradients. The abundant mitochondria of cardiac cells supply this constant ATP demand.

questions.stem: Phase 4 of the action potential corresponds to:
options: The resting (or diastolic depolarization) interval between beats
questions.explanation: In working cells, phase 4 is the stable resting potential; in nodal cells, phase 4 is the slow spontaneous (pacemaker) depolarization that leads to the next AP. Either way, it is the interval between action potentials.

questions.stem: Phase 1 of the ventricular action potential is:
options: Brief early repolarization immediately after the upstroke (transient K⁺ outflow)
questions.explanation: After the Na⁺-driven upstroke, a transient outward K⁺ current produces a short notch of partial repolarization before the plateau begins. The plateau is phase 2, not phase 1.

questions.stem: Which channels are primarily responsible for the plateau phase and for triggering sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release?
questions.explanation: L-type ("long-lasting") Ca²⁺ channels open during the plateau and admit the trigger calcium for excitation–contraction coupling. T-type channels contribute to nodal prepotentials, not the ventricular plateau.

questions.stem: Conduction velocity of the action potential along cardiac tissue depends mainly on:
options: ATP content of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The speed of the phase-0 upstroke and availability of sodium channels
questions.explanation: Faster, larger phase-0 upstrokes (more available fast Na⁺ channels) excite downstream cells sooner, increasing conduction velocity. This is why AV nodal tissue (slow Ca-driven upstroke) conducts slowly and why Na⁺-blocking drugs slow conduction.

questions.stem: Electrical conduction between adjacent cardiac cells is characterized by:
options: Low resistance and rapid spread via gap junctions
Resistance that varies with heart rate
questions.explanation: Gap junctions create low-resistance intercellular connections, so current flows quickly from cell to cell. This syncytial behavior lets the whole chamber depolarize within milliseconds.

questions.stem: The upstroke of the SA nodal action potential is slow because:
options: It is carried by slow L-type calcium channels rather than fast sodium channels
Its sodium channels open too fast
Nodal cells have no ion channels
questions.explanation: Nodal cells depolarize with calcium-driven "slow-response" APs, giving a gradual upstroke and slow conduction. Fast Na⁺ channels are unavailable at nodal resting potentials.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the phases of the ventricular action potential?
options: Upstroke (0) → early repolarization (1) → plateau (2) → repolarization (3) → rest/diastole (4)
questions.explanation: Phase 0 is the Na⁺ upstroke, phase 1 the transient notch, phase 2 the Ca²⁺ plateau, phase 3 K⁺ repolarization, and phase 4 the resting/diastolic state. Misordering these phases confuses AP interpretation.

questions.stem: The effective refractory period of the ventricular AP spans roughly:
questions.explanation: From the upstroke until Na⁺ channels recover late in phase 3, the cell cannot generate a propagated AP. Only after substantial repolarization does excitability return (relative refractory period). ---
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: The primary functional purpose of the cardiac plateau phase is to:
options: Prolong contraction and prevent tetanic contraction
questions.explanation: The plateau extends the AP and the refractory period long enough for a complete contraction–relaxation cycle, making summation/tetanus impossible and ensuring rhythmic pumping. Rapid signaling is the nerve AP's specialty.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: The nerve action potential is suited for rapid signaling because it has:
options: A very brief duration (~1–2 ms) that permits high-frequency firing
questions.explanation: Short APs and short refractory periods let nerves fire hundreds of impulses per second. Cardiac APs, in contrast, trade speed for the ability to support contraction.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: The action potential of skeletal muscle lasts approximately:
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle APs are brief (a few milliseconds), far shorter than the mechanical twitch, which allows stimuli to summate. Cardiac APs last 200–300 ms, nearly as long as the twitch itself.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: Skeletal muscle can undergo summation and tetanus because:
options: It has a prolonged refractory period
Calcium for contraction comes only from outside the cell
Its brief AP and refractory period allow successive stimuli to add tension before relaxation
questions.explanation: With APs lasting only milliseconds, repeated stimulation can overlap twitches and build fused maximal tension. The heart's long refractory period makes this impossible.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts control of cardiac and skeletal muscle?
options: Both are strictly involuntary with no neural input
Skeletal muscle is involuntary and the heart is voluntary
Cardiac muscle is involuntary with intrinsic and ANS control, while skeletal muscle is voluntary
questions.explanation: The heart beats via its intrinsic conduction system and is modulated by the autonomic nervous system; skeletal muscle requires somatic motor nerve stimulation for every contraction.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: Compared with the ventricular action potential, the SA nodal action potential has:
options: A slow calcium-driven upstroke and an unstable, spontaneously depolarizing phase 4
A rapid sodium upstroke and stable resting potential
A stable resting potential of −90 mV
questions.explanation: Nodal cells are slow-response: Ca²⁺-mediated upstroke, slow conduction, and a diastolic "prepotential" without a true resting state. Ventricular cells are fast-response with a Na⁺ upstroke and stable −90 mV phase 4.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: The rapid upstroke of the ventricular action potential is generated by:
options: Rapid sodium influx through fast Na⁺ channels
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated fast Na⁺ channels open at threshold and flood the cell with sodium, producing the steep phase-0 upstroke. Calcium channels open later and sustain the plateau.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: Relative to the ventricular action potential, the SA nodal action potential has:
options: Greater amplitude and a faster rate of rise
Lower amplitude and a slower rate of rise
questions.explanation: Calcium-driven nodal APs rise slowly from a more positive baseline and reach a lower peak, giving smaller amplitude. This is precisely why nodal conduction is slow and why the AV node delays the impulse.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: Comparing refractory periods:
options: Skeletal muscle refractory period is longer than cardiac
Skeletal muscle has no refractory period
The cardiac refractory period is much longer than the skeletal muscle refractory period
questions.explanation: The cardiac plateau keeps the heart refractory for ~250 ms, roughly the duration of the twitch itself, preventing summation. Skeletal refractory periods are only a few milliseconds.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: A toxin that selectively blocks fast voltage-gated sodium channels would have which effect on the ventricular action potential?
options: It would abolish the rapid phase-0 upstroke
questions.explanation: Without functional fast Na⁺ channels, the ventricular cell cannot generate the steep upstroke. Calcium channels are unaffected, illustrating why upstroke and plateau depend on different channel populations.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: A calcium channel blocker administered to a patient would most directly:
options: Slow SA nodal firing and AV nodal conduction
Have no cardiac effect because nodal cells lack calcium channels
questions.explanation: Nodal action potentials depend on L-type calcium channels, so blocking them slows the pacemaker prepotential and AV conduction (negative chronotropic and dromotropic effects). Nodal tissue is the most calcium-dependent tissue in the heart.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: Comparing signal speeds, the nerve action potential is:
options: Much faster overall than cardiac impulse conduction
questions.explanation: Nerve fibers conduct extremely rapidly with short APs; even the heart's fastest tissue (Purkinje, ~2–4 m/s) conducts more slowly, and the whole cardiac beat cycle takes hundreds of milliseconds.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: From an echocardiographer's perspective, the impossibility of cardiac tetany means that:
options: The heart can contract faster than it relaxes indefinitely
Summation increases stroke volume during stress
Every depolarization is followed by a full relaxation and filling period, preserving the pumping cycle
The heart can fuse contractions at high heart rates
questions.explanation: Because the long refractory period forbids summation, each beat is a complete contraction followed by relaxation and filling — the basis of rhythmic pumping. Even maximal heart rates preserve this one-contraction-per-depolarization rule.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: Which statement about the heart's independence from nerves is correct?
options: The heart requires intact nerves to beat at all
The heart contains an intrinsic pacemaker and conduction system; skeletal muscle requires nerve input to contract
Both cardiac and skeletal muscle are intrinsically rhythmic
Neither tissue can contract without autonomic nerves
questions.explanation: Autorhythmic cells generate the heartbeat without any neural input (demonstrated by transplanted or denervated hearts). Skeletal muscle, lacking automaticity, is silent until its motor nerve fires.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: The action potential feature that most directly ties electrical activity to contraction in cardiac muscle is:
options: The plateau, whose calcium influx provides the trigger for excitation–contraction coupling
questions.explanation: Calcium entering during the plateau is the same calcium that triggers SR release and contraction, making the AP itself the start of excitation–contraction coupling. This is unique to cardiac muscle.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: The total duration of a ventricular action potential is approximately:
questions.explanation: The plateau and slow repolarization stretch the ventricular AP to 200–300 ms — hundreds of times longer than nerve or skeletal muscle APs, and matched to the duration of the mechanical twitch.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: During the plateau phase, the fast sodium channels are in which state?
questions.explanation: Fast Na⁺ channels opened during phase 0 close into an inactivated state and remain unavailable throughout the plateau, which is the molecular basis of the absolute refractory period.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: Why does nodal tissue not use fast sodium channels for its upstroke?
options: Sodium is too concentrated inside the cell
Nodal cells rest at a more positive potential where fast Na⁺ channels remain inactivated
questions.explanation: Nodal maximum diastolic potential (about −60 mV) is too positive for fast Na⁺ channel availability, so depolarization falls to the slower L-type calcium channels. This defines the "slow response" AP.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: Which of the following has the shortest action potential duration?
questions.explanation: Nerve APs last only 1–2 ms. SA nodal APs are shorter than ventricular APs but still far longer than nerve APs, and Purkinje APs are the longest of all.
tags: Nodal vs Ventricular vs Nerve/Skeletal Muscle Action Potentials

questions.stem: During the plateau (phase 2), the membrane potential behavior is best described as:
options: Hovering near 0 mV while inward Ca²⁺ and outward K⁺ currents balance
questions.explanation: Balanced opposing currents hold the potential at approximately 0 mV for ~100–200 ms. Immediate return to −90 mV describes skeletal muscle repolarization, and +90 mV is unphysiologic. ---

questions.stem: With all autonomic nervous system influence removed, the SA node fires at approximately:
questions.explanation: The truly intrinsic SA nodal rate is about 100 bpm; normal resting rates (~70) exist only because of tonic vagal slowing. This distinction explains the tachycardia seen after atropine or transplantation.

questions.stem: Which site normally determines the heart rate?
questions.explanation: The SA node depolarizes to threshold fastest and therefore paces the heart; all other sites are latent pacemakers held in check by overdrive suppression.

questions.stem: The correct hierarchy of intrinsic rates from fastest to slowest is:
questions.explanation: The pacemaker hierarchy descends through the conduction system, with each successively distal site firing more slowly. The fastest site wins and normally is the SA node.

questions.stem: A junctional escape rhythm characteristically runs at:
questions.explanation: AV junctional tissue's intrinsic rate is 40–60 bpm, so junctional escapes and junctional rhythms fall in this range. Rates of 20–40 bpm belong to ventricular escapes.

questions.stem: The slowest intrinsic discharge rate of the potential pacemakers belongs to:
questions.explanation: Distal His–Purkinje tissue fires at only 20–40 bpm. It becomes the pacemaker only when both the SA node and the AV junction fail, which is why complete heart block below the His produces profound bradycardia.

questions.stem: A resting ECG at 65 bpm with a P wave before every QRS indicates a rhythm originating from the:
questions.explanation: A P wave preceding each QRS at a normal rate indicates SA nodal dominance. Junctional and ventricular rhythms lack upright sinus P waves or show dissociation.

questions.stem: "Sinus bradycardia" is best defined as:
options: Any heart rate below 60 bpm regardless of origin
Normal P waves with a rate below 60 bpm
Absent P waves with a slow rate
questions.explanation: Sinus bradycardia retains the normal SA nodal origin (P before each QRS) but at a rate under 60 bpm, often from high vagal tone. Options B and D describe escape rhythms, not a sinus mechanism.

questions.stem: "Sinus tachycardia" is best defined as:
options: A narrow-complex rhythm without P waves
A normally driven (P–QRS) rhythm exceeding 100 bpm
questions.explanation: The sinus mechanism is preserved but the SA node fires faster than 100 bpm, typically from sympathetic stimulation. Option D suggests atrial fibrillation, and option C suggests VT.

questions.stem: Heart rate rises during exercise primarily because:
options: Sympathetic stimulation steepens the slope of the SA nodal pacemaker potential
The AV node becomes the primary pacemaker
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine accelerates the prepotential so threshold is reached sooner, raising firing frequency. Vagal input simultaneously falls, releasing the node to its higher intrinsic capability.

questions.stem: An "ectopic atrial rhythm" implies that:
options: The SA node always wins under any circumstance
The ectopic focus fires slower than the SA node
An impulse source outside the SA node has become the dominant pacemaker
The ventricles are pacing the heart
questions.explanation: If an atrial focus (e.g., low atrial or wandering atrial pacemaker) reaches threshold first, it drives the rhythm, producing altered P-wave morphology. The SA node wins only when it depolarizes fastest.

questions.stem: A regular tachycardia at 120 bpm with a normal-appearing P wave before each QRS is best classified as:
questions.explanation: A regular rate above 100 bpm with a normal sinus P–QRS sequence is sinus tachycardia, typically driven by sympathetic stimulation. Atrial fibrillation is irregular, and junctional/ventricular rhythms lack sinus P waves.

questions.stem: The intrinsic firing rate of atrial (non-sinus) pacemaker sites is approximately:
questions.explanation: Atrial ectopic pacemakers fire intrinsically at roughly 60–80 bpm, just below the SA node — faster than the AV junction (40–60) but slower than the SA node's 60–100 capability.

questions.stem: The term "overdrive suppression" refers to:
options: The suppression of a slower pacemaker by the repetitive depolarizing activity of a faster one
Suppression of the heart by excess calcium
The SA node being silenced by the AV node
Autonomic shutdown of the entire conduction system
questions.explanation: A faster pacemaker keeps slower sites depolarized before they can reach their own threshold. When the fast site stops, the suppressed sites take time to recover — the basis of escape rhythms and post-tachycardia pauses.

questions.stem: A "wandering atrial pacemaker" is recognized on the ECG by:
options: Three or more different P-wave morphologies
questions.explanation: Shifting between multiple atrial foci produces at least three distinct P-wave shapes with varying PR intervals. Absent P waves suggest fibrillation or a junctional mechanism.

questions.stem: The hallmark of complete (third-degree) AV block on the ECG is:
options: Every P wave followed by a QRS
Independent atrial and ventricular activity (AV dissociation)
questions.explanation: No atrial impulse reaches the ventricles, so P waves and QRS complexes occur independently, with the QRS arising from a junctional or ventricular escape pacemaker.

questions.stem: An "escape rhythm" is defined as:
options: A rhythm caused by excess sympathetic tone
A rhythm that emerges from a latent pacemaker when faster pacemakers fail to fire or conduct
A rhythm paced by an artificial device only
questions.explanation: When the dominant pacemaker fails, the next-fastest site "escapes" suppression and takes over at its own intrinsic rate (junctional 40–60 or ventricular 20–40 bpm).

questions.stem: Myocardial ischemia promotes arrhythmias primarily because it:
options: Speeds conduction through the Purkinje system
Slows conduction and alters action potentials, creating ectopic foci and re-entry substrate
Always destroys the SA node first
questions.explanation: Ischemic cells become depolarized, conduct slowly, and develop abnormal automaticity — conditions favoring re-entry and ectopic beats. This is why arrhythmias complicate acute infarction.

questions.stem: Digitalis (digoxin) is useful for rate control in atrial fibrillation because it:
options: Slows AV nodal conduction, limiting how many atrial impulses reach the ventricles
questions.explanation: Digoxin enhances vagal tone on the AV node, whose long refractory period then filters the rapid fibrillatory impulses. The atria continue to fibrillate, but the ventricular rate falls.

questions.stem: In atrial flutter with an atrial rate of 300 bpm, a ventricular rate of exactly 150 bpm implies:
options: Complete AV conduction of every flutter wave
2:1 AV block — the AV node transmits every other beat because of its refractory period
questions.explanation: The AV node's refractory tissue cannot conduct 300 impulses per minute, so every second flutter wave is blocked. This protective filtering function is a core role of AV nodal physiology.

questions.stem: In a rapid supraventricular tachycardia, the structure that determines the maximum ventricular rate is the:
questions.explanation: All impulses from above must cross the AV node, whose conduction velocity and refractory period set the ceiling on ventricular response rate. Purkinje tissue conducts fast but only receives what the AV node passes. ---

questions.stem: The normal PR interval measures:
questions.explanation: A PR interval of 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small boxes) reflects the SA-to-ventricle conduction time dominated by AV nodal delay. Values above 0.20 s indicate first-degree AV block.

questions.stem: The normal QRS duration is:
questions.explanation: Rapid Purkinje-mediated activation completes ventricular depolarization within 0.06–0.10 s. A QRS longer than 0.12 s signals bundle branch block, ventricular origin, or other slow activation.

questions.stem: Which ECG wave is characteristically absent in atrial fibrillation?
questions.explanation: Disorganized fibrillatory activity prevents a coordinated atrial depolarization wave, so distinct P waves are replaced by an irregular fibrillatory baseline. QRS complexes remain because the AV node and ventricles still function.

questions.stem: An upright, rounded P wave in lead II suggests:
options: Origin from the SA node (normal sinus mechanism)
questions.explanation: The normal atrial activation vector travels from the SA node (high right atrium) inferiorly and leftward, producing upright P waves in lead II. Altered polarity suggests an ectopic or retrograde origin.

questions.stem: The QT interval represents:
options: Total ventricular electrical systole — depolarization plus repolarization
questions.explanation: QT spans the onset of the QRS to the end of the T wave, capturing the entire ventricular action potential duration. A lengthened QT increases susceptibility to re-entrant ventricular arrhythmias.

questions.stem: At a standard paper speed of 25 mm/s, each small ECG box represents:
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, one 1-mm small box equals 0.04 s and one large box (5 small boxes) equals 0.20 s. These conversions are essential for measuring intervals and calculating rate.

questions.stem: On a regular ECG, the R–R interval spans 4 large boxes. The heart rate is approximately:
questions.explanation: Dividing 300 by the number of large boxes (300/4) yields ~75 bpm, since each large box represents 0.2 s. This quick method applies only to regular rhythms.

questions.stem: The onset of mechanical ventricular contraction coincides most closely with which ECG component?
questions.explanation: Ventricular depolarization (QRS) triggers ventricular contraction after a brief electromechanical delay, so systole begins around the end of the QRS. The P wave drives atrial contraction and the T wave marks repolarization.

questions.stem: On an echocardiogram, aortic valve opening occurs:
options: Shortly after the QRS complex begins, as ventricular pressure rises
At the end of the T wave
questions.explanation: Electrical depolarization (QRS) precedes mechanical contraction, so ventricular pressure builds and opens the aortic valve just after the QRS. This electrical-to-mechanical lag is a consistent, predictable relationship.

questions.stem: The late-diastolic A-wave of mitral inflow on echo corresponds to which ECG event?
options: A wave occurring before the P wave
Atrial contraction following the P wave
questions.explanation: The P wave triggers atrial depolarization, and atrial contraction follows during the PR interval, producing the late-diastolic A-wave on mitral inflow Doppler. This links the electrical P wave to a measurable mechanical event.

questions.stem: On the ECG, the AV nodal delay appears as the:
options: Flat (isoelectric) PR segment between the P wave and the QRS
questions.explanation: The impulse is delayed in the small AV node, generating too little voltage to deflect the surface ECG, so the segment between P and QRS remains flat. A normal pause here is essential for ventricular filling.

questions.stem: Why is atrial repolarization not seen on the standard ECG?
options: It occurs during the resting phase
It occurs at the same time as the QRS and is masked by the larger ventricular signal
questions.explanation: Atrial repolarization happens during ventricular depolarization, and the much larger QRS complex overwhelms it. It is present electrically but not visually distinguishable.

questions.stem: The ST segment represents the period when:
options: Ventricular cells are at their resting potential
All ventricular cells are depolarized (the AP plateau), before repolarization begins
questions.explanation: During the ST segment, the ventricles are uniformly depolarized and the membrane potential sits on the plateau, so no net voltage difference appears — the segment is isoelectric. ST elevation or depression indicates injury currents.

questions.stem: A broad, notched (bifid) P wave in lead II suggests:
questions.explanation: Delayed, prolonged left atrial activation widens the P wave beyond 0.12 s and may notch it (P mitrale), classically seen in mitral valve disease — a common echo referral diagnosis.

questions.stem: At a heart rate of 60 bpm, the R–R interval measures:
questions.explanation: 60 beats per minute equals one beat every second, so the R–R interval is 1.0 s (five large boxes). The relationship is rate = 60 / R–R interval in seconds.

questions.stem: Which portion of the ECG corresponds most directly to rapid activation of the ventricles by the Purkinje system?
options: The steep upstroke and downstroke of the QRS complex
questions.explanation: The QRS deflections are produced by the fast Purkinje-mediated spread of depolarization across the ventricular mass. The slower AV nodal portion of conduction produces no visible deflection.

questions.stem: Which information can the ECG NOT provide?
questions.explanation: The ECG displays the electrical timing of activation only; it cannot show contraction, motion, or ejection. Echocardiography is the modality that visualizes the mechanical response to those electrical events.

questions.stem: The first deflection of the normal cardiac cycle on the ECG is the:
questions.explanation: The SA node fires first, so atrial depolarization (P wave) opens the cycle. No ventricular deflection can appear before atrial activation in a normally conducted beat.

questions.stem: Because contraction follows depolarization by a short electromechanical delay (~50–100 ms), echocardiographic mechanical events:
options: Slightly lag the corresponding ECG events
questions.explanation: Electrical activation must trigger calcium release and cross-bridge formation before force develops, so echo-visible events (valve opening, wall motion) consistently follow the ECG by tens of milliseconds. Understanding this lag is essential when timing echo measurements against the ECG.

questions.stem: The U wave is best described as:
options: A small deflection after the T wave, possibly representing Purkinje fiber or late myocardial repolarization
A pure artifact in every case
questions.explanation: The U wave is a low-amplitude deflection following the T wave; its origin is debated but is thought to reflect late repolarization. Prominent or inverted U waves can be clinically significant. ---
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: During the absolute refractory period:
options: A stronger-than-normal stimulus can elicit an action potential
No stimulus of any strength can elicit a propagated action potential
questions.explanation: With Na⁺ (or in nodal tissue Ca²⁺) channels fully inactivated, the membrane is completely unexcitable. Only after partial channel recovery does the relative refractory period begin.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: A premature impulse falling within the relative refractory period may:
options: Conduct slowly and potentially initiate a re-entrant arrhythmia
Be indistinguishable from a normal beat
questions.explanation: Cells in the relative refractory period respond weakly and conduct slowly, conditions that favor unidirectional block and re-entry. This is the electrophysiologic basis of many triggered and re-entrant arrhythmias.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: The classic requirements for a re-entry circuit are:
options: Transient unidirectional block, slowed conduction, and recovered (excitable) tissue ahead of the circuit
questions.explanation: An impulse must find a closed pathway with slow conduction and unidirectional block so it can circle back and re-excite recovered tissue. Ischemia, accessory pathways, and scar provide this substrate.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: An early, wide, bizarre QRS complex without a preceding P wave on the ECG is a:
questions.explanation: A ventricular focus fires early, bypassing the fast conduction system, so the QRS is early, wide, and bizarre with no sinus P wave. A PAC would be early but narrow with an abnormal preceding P wave.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: A premature narrow-QRS complex preceded by an abnormally shaped early P wave is a:
questions.explanation: The beat originates in the atria above the ventricles, so it conducts through the normal His–Purkinje system and remains narrow. The ectopic P wave distinguishes it from a junctional beat.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: The "R-on-T" phenomenon is dangerous because:
options: It is a normal finding during exercise
The impulse lands on the vulnerable relative refractory period and can precipitate ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation
questions.explanation: Stimulating the ventricle during partial repolarization creates heterogeneous excitability, the perfect substrate for re-entry. This is why PVCs falling on the T wave are treated with heightened concern.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180 bpm most likely originates:
options: Above the ventricles, with conduction through the normal His–Purkinje system (supraventricular tachycardia)
questions.explanation: A narrow QRS means ventricular activation uses the fast conduction system, which is only possible when the impulse originates above the ventricles. Ventricular rhythms activate slowly muscle-to-muscle and are wide.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: Which feature most strongly suggests ventricular tachycardia rather than SVT with aberrancy?
options: P waves always present during the tachycardia
A wide QRS with AV dissociation
questions.explanation: Wide QRS with independent atrial activity (AV dissociation) indicates a ventricular focus activating the ventricles separately from the atria. Narrow QRS argues for a supraventricular origin.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: From an echocardiography standpoint, each QRS complex on the ECG is followed by:
options: A mechanical ventricular contraction (after the electromechanical delay), unless the beat is electrically or hemodynamically ineffective
Valve closure with no wall motion
Nothing — the ECG and contraction are unrelated
questions.explanation: Depolarization initiates contraction after a short, predictable delay, so each effective QRS produces wall motion and ejection. This one-to-one electrical–mechanical coupling is what allows ECG gating of echo images.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: A wide QRS complex immediately preceded by a sharp vertical pacing spike indicates:
options: A PVC with no relation to the device
Ventricular pacing from an artificial pacemaker
Atrial pacing with intact AV conduction
questions.explanation: The spike is the pacing stimulus, and the wide QRS reflects slow, non-Purkinje activation from the pacing lead (usually in the right ventricle), mimicking a PVC pattern. Atrial pacing with intact conduction yields a narrow QRS after a stimulated P wave.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: A markedly prolonged PR interval can produce which echocardiographic finding in the mitral inflow pattern?
options: Fusion of the E and A waves, because atrial contraction occurs while ventricular filling is still finishing
Shortened diastolic filling time with separated waves
No echo change at any PR length
questions.explanation: With a long PR, the atrial contraction (A-wave) occurs while the ventricle is still relaxed and filling, so the A-wave can merge with the E-wave. This is a classic echo correlate of first-degree AV block.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: In atrial fibrillation, the mitral inflow Doppler characteristically shows:
options: A strong, organized A-wave each beat
Absence of an organized A-wave with an irregular ventricular response
A normal A-wave with regular R–R intervals
questions.explanation: Without coordinated atrial contraction there is no A-wave, and the varying R–R intervals produce beat-to-beat variation in the E-wave. This directly mirrors the electrical absence of P waves.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: The echocardiographic correlate of complete AV block is:
options: Every atrial contraction followed by ventricular contraction
Dissociation between atrial contraction and ventricular contraction
questions.explanation: Just as the ECG shows AV dissociation, echo shows atrial contractions occurring independently of ventricular contraction and valve events. The ventricles are driven by a slower escape pacemaker.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: Vagal maneuvers (e.g., carotid sinus massage) terminate some SVTs because they:
options: Increase vagal tone, slowing the SA and AV nodes and breaking the re-entry circuit
questions.explanation: Heightened vagal activity slows AV nodal conduction and prolongs its refractory period, interrupting circuits that depend on the node. This exploits the AV node's sensitivity to acetylcholine.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: The AV node protects the ventricles during atrial fibrillation because:
options: Its long refractory period filters out many of the 350–600 atrial impulses per minute
The SA node overrides the fibrillation
The ventricles remain refractory the entire time
Gap junctions block the atrial impulses
questions.explanation: Only a fraction of fibrillatory impulses find recovered AV nodal tissue and reach the ventricles, producing the characteristically "irregularly irregular" rate. Without this filtering, the ventricles could not maintain output.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: A cell that fires before the SA node depolarizes indicates:
options: Overdrive suppression by the SA node
An ectopic site with enhanced automaticity or re-entry
questions.explanation: Reaching threshold before the dominant pacemaker defines an ectopic focus. Enhanced automaticity, triggered activity, or re-entry circuits all allow non-sinus sites to capture the rhythm.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: Ischemic myocardial cells characteristically show:
options: Prolonged action potentials and faster conduction
Only mechanical changes without electrical effects
Altered (often shortened) action potentials with slowed conduction, promoting arrhythmias
questions.explanation: Hypoxia impairs pumps and channels, changing AP duration and slowing conduction — the electrophysiologic environment in which ectopy and re-entry develop. This is why arrhythmias are a leading complication of infarction.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: The complementary roles of the ECG and echocardiography are best summarized as:
options: The ECG shows valve closure and echo shows depolarization
The ECG displays electrical timing; echo displays the mechanical response
questions.explanation: The ECG records the electrical sequence (depolarization, repolarization) and its timing, while echo directly visualizes the contraction that follows. Integrating the two links electrical events to mechanical function.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: The T wave occurs mechanically closest to:
options: The end of ventricular systole, as relaxation approaches
questions.explanation: Ventricular repolarization (T wave) signals the cells returning to their resting state, coinciding with the end of contraction and the start of relaxation. Aortic valve closure occurs around the end of the T wave.
tags: Refractory Periods, Rhythm Recognition & Clinical Integration

questions.stem: Every normal heartbeat begins with:
options: Spontaneous depolarization of the SA node, initiating atrial depolarization
questions.explanation: The SA node's automatic impulse starts the entire cascade: atrial depolarization, AV delay, rapid ventricular activation, and contraction.
